pos: adj. (watchful, wakeful; required of the bishop, and commanded of every believer against the adversary)
etymology: Latin vigilans, watching, from vigil, awake. It renders Greek nephalios in 1 Timothy — sober, unmixed with wine, hence clear-headed — and gregoreo in 1 Peter, to stay awake.
biblical_def: The word stands in two lists that ought to be read together. First among the qualifications of an overseer: “A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach” (1 Timothy 3:2). The office is a good work to desire (1 Timothy 3:1), and the qualifications are almost entirely matters of character rather than gift — only apt to teach names an ability. Vigilance heads the list of dispositions because a man who is not watchful cannot guard anything, and guarding is what an overseer does. Second, the command to the whole flock: “Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:8). Peter gives the reason before he gives the remedy, and the remedy is not flight: “Whom resist stedfast in the faith, knowing that the same afflictions are accomplished in your brethren that are in the world” (1 Peter 5:9). Vigilance in Scripture is therefore never anxiety. It is the settled wakefulness of a man who knows there is a real enemy, knows the enemy is a defeated one, and does not intend to be found asleep.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines vigilant as watchful, circumspect, attentive to discover and avoid danger.
webster_full: VIGILANT, a. Watchful; circumspect; attentive to discover and avoid danger, or to provide for safety.
VIGILANCE, n. Forbearance of sleep; watchfulness.
2. Circumspection; attention of the mind in discovering and guarding against danger.
SOBER, a. Temperate in the use of spirituous liquors; habitually temperate.
2. Not mad or insane; not wild, visionary or heated with passion; having the regular exercise of cool dispassionate reason.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 3:2
A bishop then must be blameless, the husband of one wife, vigilant, sober, of good behaviour, given to hospitality, apt to teach;
1 Peter 5:8
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour:
1 Peter 5:9
Whom resist stedfast in the faith, knowing that the same afflictions are accomplished in your brethren that are in the world.
1 Timothy 3:1
This is a true saying, If a man desire the office of a bishop, he desireth a good work.
corruption_summary: Eldership is selected for competence and platform, and the one list Scripture actually gives is treated as an aspiration rather than a requirement.
corruption_paragraphs: The qualifications of 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1 are the only hiring criteria the New Testament supplies for the office, and they are overwhelmingly about a man's character, household and reputation. Modern practice regularly inverts this: churches recruit for communication, vision and administrative capacity, and treat the biblical list as a set of ideals that no one entirely meets. The text does not read as an ideal. A bishop then must be is a requirement, and the list includes a man's conduct at home, his relation to money, his temper and his sobriety. Where the list is set aside, the office is filled by men who can draw a crowd and cannot guard a flock, and the congregation discovers the difference in a crisis.

On the other side, vigilant has been enlisted for a suspicious temper that treats watchfulness as a licence to hunt heresy in every brother. Peter's vigilance is directed at a named adversary, and the same chapter tells elders to feed the flock willingly and not as lords over God's heritage. A watchman who spends his wakefulness on his own people rather than on the enemy has mistaken his post. Vigilance guards the sheep; it does not stalk them.
roots_summary: Greek nephalios (G3524), sober and watchful — 1 Timothy 3:2, 3:11, Titus 2:2; gregoreo (G1127), to be awake — 1 Peter 5:8, Matthew 26:41.
roots_lines: Greek nephalios (G3524) — sober, vigilant; 1 Timothy 3:2, 3:11 and Titus 2:2, always in a list of qualifications.
Greek gregoreo (G1127) — to stay awake, to watch; 1 Peter 5:8, and the Lord's word in Gethsemane, watch and pray.
Greek episkopos (G1985) — overseer, bishop; 1 Timothy 3:2, one office with elder and pastor.
Greek antidikos (G476) — an opponent in a lawsuit, an adversary; 1 Peter 5:8, of the devil.
1 Peter 5:9 supplies the posture: resist stedfast in the faith — not flight, and not fear.
usage: “A bishop then must be… vigilant” — a requirement, not an aspiration.
“Be sober, be vigilant” — because the adversary is real and already defeated.
A man who is not watchful cannot guard anything.

pos: adj. (self-pleasing, governed by one's own will; expressly disqualifying in an elder)
etymology: The Authorized Version's compound for Greek authades — from autos (self) and hedomai (to please) — one who pleases himself, arrogant, unaccommodating. The English keeps the sense exactly: a will that answers to itself.
biblical_def: “For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre” (Titus 1:7). The disqualification is placed immediately after the word steward, and that is the argument. A steward manages what belongs to another; a selfwilled man manages what belongs to another as though it belonged to him. Paul then gives the positive side: “But a lover of hospitality, a lover of good men, sober, just, holy, temperate” (Titus 1:8), and requires him to hold fast the faithful word so that he can exhort and convince the gainsayers (Titus 1:9). The only other occurrence of the word is a description of false teachers: “Presumptuous are they, selfwilled, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities” (2 Peter 2:10). Peter sharpens it by contrast in the next verse — angels, who are greater in power and might, “bring not railing accusation against them before the Lord” (2 Peter 2:11). The selfwilled man is bolder than an angel and has less warrant.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines self-willed as governed by one's own will, not yielding to the will or wishes of others, obstinate.
webster_full: SELF-WILLED, a. Governed by one's own will; not yielding to the will of others; obstinate.
SELF-WILL, n. One's own will; obstinacy.
STEWARD, n. A man employed in great families to manage the domestic concerns, superintend the other servants, and receive and pay money.
PRESUMPTUOUS, a. Bold and confident to excess; adventuring without reasonable ground of success.
OBSTINATE, a. Stubborn; fixed firmly in resolution or opinion; not yielding to reason or persuasion.
scriptures: Titus 1:7
For a bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled, not soon angry, not given to wine, no striker, not given to filthy lucre;
2 Peter 2:10
But chiefly them that walk after the flesh in the lust of uncleanness, and despise government. Presumptuous are they, selfwilled, they are not afraid to speak evil of dignities.
Titus 1:8
But a lover of hospitality, a lover of good men, sober, just, holy, temperate;
2 Peter 2:11
Whereas angels, which are greater in power and might, bring not railing accusation against them before the Lord.
corruption_summary: Self-will is rebranded as strong leadership, and the very trait Scripture bars from the office becomes the reason a man is given it.
corruption_paragraphs: The contemporary vocabulary of church leadership — vision, decisiveness, the willingness to make hard calls without consensus — describes something Scripture may commend and something Scripture expressly forbids, and the two are almost impossible to tell apart from the outside. Titus 1:7 supplies the test, and it is the word steward. A steward has authority and the authority is delegated; he answers for the estate to someone else. A man who cannot be told anything, who treats the plurality of elders as an obstacle, and whose congregation has learned that disagreement is disloyalty, is not a strong leader with rough edges. He is disqualified by the text, whatever the church has grown to.

The plurality of elders is the structural safeguard the New Testament provides against exactly this, and it is the safeguard most often quietly dismantled — retained on paper while one man's will decides everything of consequence. Peter's picture is the check on the other end: angels greater in power do not bring railing accusation, and the selfwilled teacher does. Boldness is not evidence of authority. The measure of a steward is whether he can be corrected by the Word and by the brethren the Lord has set beside him.
roots_summary: Greek authades (G829), self-pleasing — Titus 1:7, 2 Peter 2:10; contrasted with oikonomos (G3623), a steward — Titus 1:7.
roots_lines: Greek authades (G829) — self-pleasing, arrogant; only Titus 1:7 and 2 Peter 2:10, and disqualifying in both.
Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a house-manager, steward; Titus 1:7, 1 Corinthians 4:1-2, where the requirement is faithfulness.
Greek tolmetes (G5113) — a daring man, presumptuous; 2 Peter 2:10, joined to authades.
Greek plektes (G4131) — a striker; Titus 1:7 and 1 Timothy 3:3, the physical companion of a self-pleasing temper.
Titus 1:8 gives the positive portrait the negative list is measured against — hospitable, sober, just, holy, temperate.
usage: “A bishop must be blameless, as the steward of God; not selfwilled” — the steward is the test.
“Presumptuous are they, selfwilled” — the mark of the false teacher.
Angels greater in power bring no railing accusation; the selfwilled man does.

pos: adj. (compassionate, easily moved to pity; commanded of believers, and in Chronicles a term for a young king's weakness)
etymology: From tender (Latin tener, soft) and heart. The Greek in Ephesians is eusplagchnos — literally well-bowelled, from the seat of the affections in Hebrew and Greek idiom; the bowels of mercies of Colossians 3:12.
biblical_def: “And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you” (Ephesians 4:32). The verse is the second half of a pair, and the first half must be read with it: “Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice” (Ephesians 4:31). Paul does not command an emotion in a vacuum; he commands the removal of what hardens a man and the putting on of what softens him, and he grounds the whole in the forgiveness already received. The measure is not the offender's worth but God's mercy in Christ. Colossians states the same duty in the older idiom: “Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering” (Colossians 3:12). One Old Testament use runs the other way and is worth noticing: Rehoboam “was young and tenderhearted, and could not withstand them” (2 Chronicles 13:7). There the word describes a softness that could not stand up to wicked men. Scripture therefore commends tenderness of heart and warns against softness of spine, and they are not the same thing.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines tender-hearted as having great sensibility, susceptible of impressions or influence, compassionate.
webster_full: TENDER-HEARTED, a. Having great sensibility; susceptible of impressions or influence; compassionate.
TENDER, a. Easily impressed, broken, bruised or injured; not firm or hard.
2. Having great sensibility; easily pained; susceptible of the softer passions, as love, compassion, kindness.
COMPASSION, n. A suffering with another; painful sympathy; a sensation of sorrow excited by the distress or misfortunes of another.
BOWELS, n. The interior part; hence, tenderness, pity, compassion.
scriptures: Ephesians 4:32
And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
Ephesians 4:31
Let all bitterness, and wrath, and anger, and clamour, and evil speaking, be put away from you, with all malice:
Colossians 3:12
Put on therefore, as the elect of God, holy and beloved, bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind, meekness, longsuffering;
2 Chronicles 13:7

And there are gathered unto him vain men, the children of Belial, and have strengthened themselves against Rehoboam the son of Solomon, when Rehoboam was young and tenderhearted, and could not withstand them.
corruption_summary: Tenderness is either dismissed as weakness by men who want to be hard, or inflated into an unwillingness to confront anything at all.
corruption_paragraphs: A strain of contemporary teaching on manhood treats compassion as something to be trained out — strength defined as hardness, and tenderness as a quality proper to women and children. Ephesians 4:32 is addressed to a whole congregation, men included, and the Lord who is its pattern was moved with compassion again and again while never once retreating from a hard word to the Pharisees. The bowels of mercies are commanded of the elect of God without exception. A man who has hardened himself has not become strong; he has disobeyed a plain apostolic command and lost the capacity to forgive as he has been forgiven.

The opposite corruption uses tenderheartedness to forbid all correction, so that any confrontation is unkindness by definition. Rehoboam is the warning at that end: young and tenderhearted, and unable to withstand the children of Belial. The same epistle that commands tenderness commands elders to convince the gainsayers and the church to have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness. Tenderness of heart toward persons and firmness toward sin belong together in Scripture, and a church that cannot hold both will lose the tenderness first and then the truth.
roots_summary: Greek eusplagchnos (G2155), tenderhearted — Ephesians 4:32, 1 Peter 3:8; splagchna oiktirmou, bowels of mercies — Colossians 3:12; Hebrew rak lebab, tender of heart — 2 Chronicles 13:7.
roots_lines: Greek eusplagchnos (G2155) — tenderhearted, compassionate; Ephesians 4:32 and 1 Peter 3:8 only.
Greek splagchnon (G4698) — the inward parts, hence the affections; the bowels of mercies of Colossians 3:12.
Greek chrestos (G5543) — kind, gracious; Ephesians 4:32, joined to tenderheartedness, and used of the Lord's easy yoke.
Hebrew rak — tender, soft; 2 Chronicles 13:7 of Rehoboam, where softness could not withstand wicked men.
Ephesians 4:32 fixes the measure: forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you.
usage: “Be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another” — and the ground follows.
“Bowels of mercies, kindness, humbleness of mind” — put on as the elect of God.
Rehoboam was tenderhearted and could not withstand — tenderness is not spinelessness.

pos: adj. (not liable to censure; the condition in which Christ will present His people, and the manner of a faithful ministry)
etymology: From un- and blameable, rendering Greek amomos (without spot, a sacrificial term) and amemptos (without ground of complaint). The first speaks of what a thing is; the second of what can be charged against it.
biblical_def: “In the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and unblameable and unreproveable in his sight” (Colossians 1:22). The three adjectives are the goal of the reconciliation described in the verse before, and the means is named without ambiguity — the body of His flesh through death. This is not a standard set for the believer to reach but a condition Christ undertakes to produce, and the sacrificial word amomos is the one used of a lamb without blemish. Paul prays for the same thing over the Thessalonians: “To the end he may stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness before God, even our Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints” (1 Thessalonians 3:13), and closes the epistle with the prayer that their whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless (1 Thessalonians 5:23) — a work he attributes to the God of peace, not to their effort. There is also a present sense, used of conduct: “Ye are witnesses, and God also, how holily and justly and unblameably we behaved ourselves among you that believe” (1 Thessalonians 2:10). Paul could say that of his ministry, and the claim is not sinlessness but a life against which no just charge could be laid.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines unblamable as not blamable, upright, innocent, not deserving censure.
webster_full: UNBLAMABLE, a. Not blamable; not culpable; innocent.
UNBLAMABLY, adv. In a manner not to incur blame.
BLAMELESS, a. Without fault; innocent; guiltless; not meriting censure.
UNREPROVABLE, a. Not deserving reproof.
PRESENT, v.t. To set, place or introduce before or in the presence of a superior.
scriptures: Colossians 1:22
In the body of his flesh through death, to present you holy and unblameable and unreproveable in his sight:
1 Thessalonians 3:13
To the end he may stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness before God, even our Father, at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ with all his saints.
1 Thessalonians 2:10
Ye are witnesses, and God also, how holily and justly and unblameably we behaved ourselves among you that believe:
1 Thessalonians 5:23
And the very God of peace sanctify you wholly; and I pray God your whole spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless unto the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ.
corruption_summary: A word describing what Christ will make of His people is read as a standard they must achieve, and assurance dies under it.
corruption_paragraphs: Colossians 1:22 is regularly preached as an exhortation — be unblameable, so that you may be presented so. The grammar is against it. Christ is the subject of the presenting, the reconciled are the object, and the instrument is the body of His flesh through death. The same pattern holds in 1 Thessalonians, where Paul does not tell them to preserve themselves blameless but prays that the God of peace would preserve them. Turn the promise into a requirement and the perfectionist and the despairing conscience both follow inevitably: one man claims he has arrived, the other concludes he never will.

The opposite error takes the imputed standing as though it made present conduct indifferent, which 1 Thessalonians 2:10 forbids by example. Paul appeals to the Thessalonians and to God as witnesses of how he behaved among them — holily, justly, unblameably. A minister able to say that is not claiming perfection; he is claiming that his life would bear inspection. The Reformed order keeps the two together in their right places: unblameable before God by the imputed righteousness of Christ, and unblameable before men by a life the Spirit is actually changing.
roots_summary: Greek amomos (G299), without blemish — Colossians 1:22, Ephesians 1:4; amemptos (G273), without ground of blame — 1 Thessalonians 3:13, Philippians 3:6.
roots_lines: Greek amomos (G299) — unblemished, a sacrificial term; Colossians 1:22, Ephesians 1:4, 1 Peter 1:19 of the Lamb Himself.
Greek amemptos (G273) — blameless, without just charge; 1 Thessalonians 3:13, and Philippians 3:6 of Paul's former standing in the law.
Greek anegkletos (G410) — unreproveable, unaccused; Colossians 1:22, and required of elders and deacons in 1 Timothy 3:10, Titus 1:6.
Greek paristemi (G3936) — to present, to set beside; Colossians 1:22, of what Christ does with His people.
1 Peter 1:19 shows why the sacrificial word fits: a lamb without blemish and without spot, and His people are made like Him.
usage: “To present you holy and unblameable and unreproveable in his sight” — He presents; we are presented.
“Stablish your hearts unblameable in holiness” — a prayer, not a demand.
“How holily and justly and unblameably we behaved ourselves” — a life that bore inspection.

pos: adj. (acceptable, giving satisfaction; of sacrifices and of obedience that God receives)
etymology: The Authorized Version's compound for Greek euarestos — from eu (well) and arestos (pleasing). The related verb is used of Enoch, who before his translation had this testimony, that he pleased God.
biblical_def: Paul uses the word of a gift sent to him in prison by a poor church: “But I have all, and abound: I am full, having received of Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God” (Philippians 4:18). The vocabulary is the vocabulary of the altar — a sweet savour, a sacrifice — applied to money given to support a preacher. Hebrews then uses it in the great benediction: the God of peace “Make you perfect in every good work to do his will, working in you that which is wellpleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ” (Hebrews 13:21). Two things in that sentence prevent any doctrine of self-improvement. God is the one working in you, and the acceptance is through Jesus Christ. Whatever is wellpleasing in the believer, God Himself produced it and Christ presents it. Paul draws the same conclusion for the whole of life: “that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service” (Romans 12:1). The believer's ordinary obedience is not a lesser thing than the temple offerings; it is what those offerings pointed toward.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines well-pleasing as pleasing in a high degree, acceptable, and acceptable as pleasing or agreeable to a receiver.
webster_full: WELL-PLEASING, a. Pleasing in a high degree; acceptable.
ACCEPTABLE, a. That may be received with pleasure; hence pleasing to a receiver; gratifying.
SAVOR, n. Taste or odor; something that perceptibly affects the organs of taste and smell.
SACRIFICE, n. An offering made to God on an altar, by means of a regular liturgy.
2. Destruction, surrender or loss made or incurred for gaining some object.
scriptures: Philippians 4:18
But I have all, and abound: I am full, having received of Epaphroditus the things which were sent from you, an odour of a sweet smell, a sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God.
Hebrews 13:21
Make you perfect in every good work to do his will, working in you that which is wellpleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ; to whom be glory for ever and ever. Amen.
Romans 12:1
I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service.
Hebrews 13:20
Now the God of peace, that brought again from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great shepherd of the sheep, through the blood of the everlasting covenant,
corruption_summary: Pleasing God is turned into a transaction that earns His favour, or dismissed altogether as though grace made obedience irrelevant.
corruption_paragraphs: The idea that a Christian may do what is wellpleasing to God has been made to carry a weight it cannot bear, as though the believer's acceptance rose and fell with his performance. Hebrews 13:21 rules that out in its own clause structure: the good work is God working in us, and its acceptability is through Jesus Christ. The Father is not weighing the offering on its own merits. He receives it in the Son, which is why a small gift from a poor congregation at Philippi could be called a sacrifice of a sweet smell. Justified men please God; they do not procure their justification by pleasing Him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word. The principle to recover is that God is genuinely pleased with the obedience of His children. A reaction against merit-theology has produced preaching in which nothing the believer does matters at all, and the effect is to leave Christians with no motive but gratitude in the abstract and no sense that the Father delights in a son's obedience. Scripture is warmer than that. Enoch had this testimony, that he pleased God; the Philippians' gift was a sweet savour; and the words well done are spoken at the end to servants whose faithfulness was itself the gift of grace.
roots_summary: Greek euarestos (G2101), wellpleasing — Philippians 4:18, Hebrews 13:21, Romans 12:1-2; the verb euaresteo (G2100) — Hebrews 11:5-6.
roots_lines: Greek euarestos (G2101) — wellpleasing, acceptable; Romans 12:1, Philippians 4:18, Hebrews 13:21, Colossians 3:20.
Greek euaresteo (G2100) — to please well; Hebrews 11:5 of Enoch, and Hebrews 11:6, that without faith it is impossible to please him.
Greek osme euodias — an odour of a sweet smell; Philippians 4:18, the language of Leviticus applied to a church's gift.
Greek katartizo (G2675) — to make complete, to mend; Hebrews 13:21, rendered make you perfect.
Hebrews 11:6 sets the condition: without faith it is impossible to please him.
usage: “A sacrifice acceptable, wellpleasing to God” — said of money sent to a prisoner.
“Working in you that which is wellpleasing in his sight, through Jesus Christ” — God works it, Christ presents it.
Justified men please God; they do not buy their justification with it.

pos: v.t. (to overturn from the foundation; used of false teachers overturning households and hearers)
etymology: Latin subvertere, to turn from beneath, to overthrow. It renders Greek anatrepo (to turn upside down) in Titus, anaskeuazo (to dismantle, as an army breaking camp) in Acts, and katastrophe (an overturning) in 2 Timothy.
biblical_def: Paul's charge against the Cretan false teachers is blunt: “Whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre's sake” (Titus 1:11). The unit overturned is the house — the family, not merely the individual — and the motive is money. The Jerusalem letter uses the same idea of the circumcision party: “certain which went out from us have troubled you with words, subverting your souls, saying, Ye must be circumcised, and keep the law: to whom we gave no such commandment” (Acts 15:24). And Paul warns Timothy that even the manner of teaching can do it: they are to be charged “that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers” (2 Timothy 2:14). Word-wrangling is not harmless; it dismantles the people who listen to it. The remedy in Titus is not argument alone but a qualified eldership holding fast the faithful word, “that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers” (Titus 1:9). Lamentations adds the divine judgment on the practice in the civil sphere: “To subvert a man in his cause, the Lord approveth not” (Lamentations 3:36).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines subvert as to overthrow from the foundation, to ruin utterly, to corrupt or confound.
webster_full: SUBVERT, v.t. To overthrow from the foundation; to overturn; to ruin utterly.
2. To corrupt; to confound; to pervert the mind, and turn it from the truth.
SUBVERSION, n. Entire overthrow; ruin; utter destruction.
GAINSAYER, n. One who contradicts or denies what is alleged; an opposer.
LUCRE, n. Gain in money or goods; profit; usually in an ill sense, or with a sense of something base or unworthy.
scriptures: Titus 1:11
Whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre's sake.
Acts 15:24

Forasmuch as we have heard, that certain which went out from us have troubled you with words, subverting your souls, saying, Ye must be circumcised, and keep the law: to whom we gave no such commandment:
2 Timothy 2:14
Of these things put them in remembrance, charging them before the Lord that they strive not about words to no profit, but to the subverting of the hearers.
Titus 1:9
Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
corruption_summary: The apostolic command to stop the mouths of false teachers is treated as intolerance, while the households they overturn are counted acceptable losses.
corruption_paragraphs: Whose mouths must be stopped is among the least congenial sentences in the Pastorals for a church shaped by the assumption that every position deserves a platform. Paul is not describing debate; he is describing damage — whole houses overturned for money — and prescribing that the teaching be silenced in the congregation. This is not a licence for the suppression of honest disagreement among brethren, and Titus 1:9 shows the ordinary instrument is sound doctrine well taught. But a church that will not finally say this may not be taught here has no way to protect the families in its care, and the New Testament plainly expects elders to say it.

The second thing usually missed is the unit Paul names. Not individuals but whole houses, and the same domestic focus appears in 2 Timothy 3:6 with those who creep into houses. False teaching does its worst work at the level of the family, which is precisely where modern ministry is least equipped to notice it: children catechised by whatever the household consumes, a father's convictions quietly reversed, and no one in the church aware until the family is gone. The remedy Scripture gives is domestic as well as ecclesial — fathers teaching their own households, and elders who know the houses they oversee.
roots_summary: Greek anatrepo (G396), to overturn — Titus 1:11, 2 Timothy 2:18; anaskeuazo (G384), to dismantle — Acts 15:24; katastrophe (G2692), an overthrow — 2 Timothy 2:14.
roots_lines: Greek anatrepo (G396) — to overturn; Titus 1:11 of whole houses, 2 Timothy 2:18 of overthrowing the faith of some.
Greek anaskeuazo (G384) — to pack up and carry off, to dismantle; Acts 15:24, its only occurrence, of subverting souls.
Greek katastrophe (G2692) — an overturning, catastrophe; 2 Timothy 2:14, of what word-strife does to hearers.
Greek epistomizo (G1993) — to stop the mouth, as with a bridle; Titus 1:11, its only occurrence.
Titus 1:9 names the ordinary instrument: sound doctrine, able both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers.
usage: “Who subvert whole houses… for filthy lucre's sake” — the unit is the family, the motive is money.
“Subverting your souls” — what the circumcision party did with words.
“Strive not about words… to the subverting of the hearers” — word-wrangling is not harmless.

pos: n. pl. (those given to speech; in Titus, the vain talkers whose religion is words without works)
etymology: From talk, of Germanic origin. Titus 1:10 renders the Greek mataiologos — from mataios (empty, futile) and logos (word) — an empty-word man, one whose speech carries nothing.
biblical_def: “For there are many unruly and vain talkers and deceivers, specially they of the circumcision” (Titus 1:10). The three nouns build: unruly, meaning not subject to the order of the church; vain talkers, whose words are hollow; deceivers, which is what hollow words become when they are believed. The next verse gives their effect and their motive — they subvert whole houses for filthy lucre's sake — so this is not a complaint about men who talk too much but about a ministry of empty speech that does real damage. Paul warns Timothy about the same pattern in another form: younger widows “learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not” (1 Timothy 5:13). Ezekiel supplies the Old Testament use, where the talkers are outside and the covenant people are their subject: Israel is “taken up in the lips of talkers, and are an infamy of the people” (Ezekiel 36:3). The chapter that follows that indictment is the promise of a new heart and a new spirit — God's answer to the reproach is not a better reputation but a changed people.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a talker as one who talks, and especially a loquacious person, a prattler, a boaster of what he will do.
webster_full: TALKER, n. One who talks; also, a loquacious person, male or female; a prattler.
2. A boaster; a braggart; used by Shakespeare, but not now so applied.
VAIN, a. Empty; worthless; having no substance, value or importance.
TATTLER, n. One who tattles; an idle talker; one who tells tales.
BUSYBODY, n. One who officiously concerns himself with the affairs of others; a meddling person.
scriptures: Titus 1:10
For there are many unruly and vain talkers and deceivers, specially they of the circumcision:
Titus 1:11
Whose mouths must be stopped, who subvert whole houses, teaching things which they ought not, for filthy lucre's sake.
1 Timothy 5:13
And withal they learn to be idle, wandering about from house to house; and not only idle, but tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not.
Ezekiel 36:3

Therefore prophesy and say, Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because they have made you desolate, and swallowed you up on every side, that ye might be a possession unto the residue of the heathen, and ye are taken up in the lips of talkers, and are an infamy of the people:
corruption_summary: The church has built its platforms on the very gift Scripture treats with suspicion, and fluency now passes for faithfulness.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture is markedly unimpressed by verbal facility. Titus 1:10 puts vain talkers among the unruly and the deceivers; James warns that not many should be masters, knowing they receive the greater condemnation; and Paul reminds the Corinthians that the kingdom of God is not in word but in power. The modern arrangement runs the other way: influence follows the microphone, and the men most heard are those most able to talk. A ministry is not tested by the size of its audience or the quality of its phrases but by whether the households under it are being built up or quietly overturned. Fluency is a gift and it is not a qualification; the list in Titus 1 requires a man's life, and asks only that he be apt to teach.

1 Timothy 5:13 names the domestic form, and it should be read without the condescension it usually receives. Paul's concern is idleness turning into speech that circulates through households doing harm — and the same pattern operates now with far greater reach, in a congregation where anyone may broadcast to everyone. The biblical categories here are plain ones: talebearing, meddling, speaking things which they ought not. They are sins of the tongue, they wreck churches, and the remedy Paul gives is not silence but useful work.
roots_summary: Greek mataiologos (G3151), a vain talker — Titus 1:10, its only occurrence; phluaros (G5397), a tattler — 1 Timothy 5:13.
roots_lines: Greek mataiologos (G3151) — an empty talker; Titus 1:10, its only occurrence in the New Testament.
Greek mataiologia (G3150) — vain jangling; 1 Timothy 1:6, of those who turned aside from charity out of a pure heart.
Greek anupotaktos (G506) — unruly, not subject; Titus 1:10, and Titus 1:6 of children who must not be so.
Greek phluaros (G5397) — a babbler, tattler; 1 Timothy 5:13, its only occurrence.
Ezekiel 36:3 shows the covenant people as the subject of the talkers, and Ezekiel 36:26 gives God's answer — a new heart.
usage: “Many unruly and vain talkers and deceivers” — the three nouns build on one another.
“Tattlers also and busybodies, speaking things which they ought not” — the domestic form.
Fluency is a gift; it was never a qualification.

pos: adj. (careless, neglecting duty; forbidden to those appointed to God's service and to those entrusted with the truth)
etymology: Latin negligens, from nec (not) and legere (to gather, to heed) — not gathering up, not attending to. The sin it names is not an act but an omission.
biblical_def: Hezekiah's charge to the Levites at the cleansing of the temple sets the tone: “My sons, be not now negligent: for the LORD hath chosen you to stand before him, to serve him, and that ye should minister unto him, and burn incense” (2 Chronicles 29:11). The ground of the warning is election to service — the LORD hath chosen you — and being chosen is precisely why negligence is intolerable. Peter takes the same word for his own resolve as a dying apostle: “Wherefore I will not be negligent to put you always in remembrance of these things, though ye know them, and be established in the present truth” (2 Peter 1:12). Note what he refuses to neglect: not new material, but reminding a congregation of what they already know and are already established in. He adds that he will keep at it as long as he is in this tabernacle (2 Peter 1:13). The gravest use is the writer to the Hebrews putting the question to those who let the gospel slide: “How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation” (Hebrews 2:3). No hostility is required to be lost. Neglect is sufficient.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines negligent as careless, heedless, apt to omit what ought to be done, and negligence as habitual omission of that which ought to be done.
webster_full: NEGLIGENT, a. Careless; heedless; apt or accustomed to omit what ought to be done.
2. Regardless.
NEGLIGENCE, n. Neglect; omission to do what ought to be done; habitual omission of that which ought to be done.
NEGLECT, v.t. To omit by carelessness or design; to forbear to do, use, employ, promote or attend to.
REMEMBRANCE, n. The retaining or having in mind the idea of a thing which has been known.
scriptures: 2 Chronicles 29:11
My sons, be not now negligent: for the LORD hath chosen you to stand before him, to serve him, and that ye should minister unto him, and burn incense.
2 Peter 1:12
Wherefore I will not be negligent to put you always in remembrance of these things, though ye know them, and be established in the present truth.
Hebrews 2:3
How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation; which at the first began to be spoken by the Lord, and was confirmed unto us by them that heard him;
2 Peter 1:13
Yea, I think it meet, as long as I am in this tabernacle, to stir you up by putting you in remembrance;
corruption_summary: Sins of omission are barely counted as sins, and a soul is lost by drifting rather than by deciding.
corruption_paragraphs: Most accounting of sin, in preaching and in private conscience, deals in things done. Scripture is at least as concerned with things left undone, and Hebrews 2:3 puts the sharpest question in the New Testament to the merely careless: how shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation. The verse does not describe a man who rejected Christ after weighing the claim; it describes a man who let the matter slip — the previous verse warns of letting the things heard slip away like a boat from its moorings. Apostasy is rarely a decision. It is generally a slow inattention, and the church that only ever warns against unbelief has left the more common road unmarked.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Peter's: a faithful ministry is largely the refusal to be negligent about what the congregation already knows. He writes to people established in the present truth and announces that he will not stop reminding them of it while he lives. That is the opposite of the appetite for novelty which drives so much teaching — the assumption that a congregation which has heard a doctrine has therefore been fed it. Repetition of settled truth is not a failure of imagination in a preacher; it is the apostolic pattern, and Peter treats it as the last duty of a dying man.
roots_summary: Hebrew shalah, to be negligent or at ease — 2 Chronicles 29:11; Greek ameleo (G272), to be careless of — 2 Peter 1:12, Hebrews 2:3, 1 Timothy 4:14.
roots_lines: Hebrew shalah — to be at ease, hence to be negligent; 2 Chronicles 29:11, Hezekiah's charge to the Levites.
Greek ameleo (G272) — to be careless of, to neglect; Hebrews 2:3, 2 Peter 1:12, and 1 Timothy 4:14 of neglecting the gift.
Greek pararrheo (G3901) — to flow past, to slip away; Hebrews 2:1, the drifting that verse 3 calls neglect.
Greek hupomimnesko (G5279) — to put in remembrance; 2 Peter 1:12, the duty Peter would not neglect.
2 Peter 1:15 shows the aim: that they might be able after his decease to have these things always in remembrance.
usage: “Be not now negligent: for the LORD hath chosen you” — election is the reason, not the excuse.
“How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation” — no hostility is required to be lost.
“I will not be negligent to put you always in remembrance” — repetition is the apostolic pattern.

pos: adj. (belonging to the natural life of the soul apart from the Spirit; in James and Jude, one of three descending terms for false wisdom)
etymology: Latin sensualis, of the senses. In James 3:15 and Jude 19 it renders Greek psuchikos — from psuche, the soul — the merely natural man's faculty, as distinguished from pneumatikos, spiritual. The English has narrowed since 1611 toward bodily appetite; the Greek is broader and worse.
biblical_def: James is contrasting two wisdoms, and he grades the false one in three steps: “This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish” (James 3:15). Earthly — its horizon is this world. Sensual — it operates by the unregenerate soul's own resources. Devilish — it finally shares the character of demons. The context is not bodily indulgence at all but envying and strife in a congregation: “For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work” (James 3:16). Against it stands the wisdom from above, which is “first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy” (James 3:17). Jude uses the word of men inside the church: “These be they who separate themselves, sensual, having not the Spirit” (Jude 1:19). The last clause is the definition — sensual means having not the Spirit. A man may be clever, religious, and morally restrained, and be psuchikos: possessing soul and body and lacking the one thing that makes a man spiritual.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sensual as pertaining to the senses as distinct from the mind, devoted to the gratification of appetite, and in theology carnal, opposed to spiritual.
webster_full: SENSUAL, a. Pertaining to the senses, as distinct from the mind or soul.
2. Consisting in sense, or depending on it; as sensual appetites.
3. Devoted to the gratification of sense; carnal.
4. In theology, carnal; pertaining to the flesh or body, in opposition to the spirit; not spiritual or holy.
CARNAL, a. Fleshly; pertaining to flesh; opposed to spiritual.
scriptures: James 3:15
This wisdom descendeth not from above, but is earthly, sensual, devilish.
Jude 1:19
These be they who separate themselves, sensual, having not the Spirit.
James 3:16
For where envying and strife is, there is confusion and every evil work.
James 3:17
But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, and easy to be intreated, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.
corruption_summary: The word is read as bodily indulgence only, which lets respectable men who are wholly natural believe the verse is about someone else.
corruption_paragraphs: The English word has drifted since 1611. Read sensual as sexual appetite and James 3:15 becomes a warning to the openly debauched, which lets everyone else off. The Greek psuchikos is the same word Paul uses in 1 Corinthians 2:14 for the natural man who receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God, and it names an entire mode of existence: soul and body operating without the Spirit. On that reading the verse lands where James aimed it — on ambitious, bitter, disputatious men in a church, whose conduct is outwardly respectable and whose wisdom is earthly, sensual and devilish. That is a far more searching text than the one usually preached from it.

Jude's clause makes the definition unmistakable: sensual, having not the Spirit. This cuts against a common assumption that the difference between a Christian and a non-Christian is a difference of behaviour or sincerity. Scripture puts the difference somewhere else entirely — the possession of the Spirit of Christ, without which a man is none of His. It also warns that such men are found inside the assembly, separating themselves, and that the mark is not gross scandal but the absence of what cannot be counterfeited.
roots_summary: Greek psuchikos (G5591), of the natural soul — James 3:15, Jude 19, 1 Corinthians 2:14, 15:44; set against pneumatikos (G4152), spiritual.
roots_lines: Greek psuchikos (G5591) — belonging to the soul, natural; James 3:15, Jude 19, 1 Corinthians 2:14, 1 Corinthians 15:44, 46.
Greek pneumatikos (G4152) — spiritual; the term psuchikos is everywhere set against, most sharply in 1 Corinthians 2:14-15.
Greek epigeios (G1919) — earthly; James 3:15, the first of the three descending terms.
Greek daimoniodes (G1141) — devilish, demon-like; James 3:15, its only occurrence, and the last step down.
1 Corinthians 2:14 gives the plain definition: the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness unto him.
usage: “Earthly, sensual, devilish” — three descending steps, and the subject is envying and strife.
“Sensual, having not the Spirit” — Jude's definition of the term.
The natural man may be clever, moral, and religious, and still be psuchikos.

pos: n. (discord, dissension; listed among the works of the flesh, and named as an effect of Christ's coming in a divided household)
etymology: Latin variantia, difference, from variare, to change or differ. In Galatians it renders Greek eris, strife or contention; in Matthew it renders dichazo, to cut in two, to set at odds.
biblical_def: Variance stands in the catalogue of the works of the flesh: “Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies” (Galatians 5:20). The list begins with adultery and uncleanness (Galatians 5:19), and the placement is instructive — the sins of division sit in the same catalogue as the sins of the body, and outnumber them. Against the whole list stands the single ninefold fruit: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith” (Galatians 5:22). The other use is the Lord's own, and it is not a work of the flesh at all: “For I am come to set a man at variance against his father, and the daughter against her mother, and the daughter in law against her mother in law” (Matthew 10:35). He is not commending discord; He is telling the truth about what following Him costs in a divided house. The two uses must be kept apart. Variance that arises from the flesh — from envy, ambition and temper — is sin. Variance that arises because one member of a family has bowed to Christ and the others will not is the price of confessing Him, and He warns of it plainly so that no one is taken by surprise.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines variance as disagreement, dissension, discord, and in law an alteration of something laid in the writ.
webster_full: VARIANCE, n. In law, an alteration of something formerly laid in a writ.
2. Disagreement; difference; discord; dissension; a falling out.
3. At variance, in disagreement; in a state of dissension or controversy; at enmity.
DISCORD, n. Disagreement among persons or things; difference of opinion; variance; opposition.
CONTENTION, n. Strife; struggle; a violent effort to obtain something, or to resist a person or claim.
scriptures: Galatians 5:20
Idolatry, witchcraft, hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies,
Galatians 5:19
Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are these; Adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lasciviousness,
Galatians 5:22
But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith,
Matthew 10:35
For I am come to set a man at variance against his father, and the daughter against her mother, and the daughter in law against her mother in law.
corruption_summary: The divisive sins in Galatians 5 are quietly excused as personality, while Matthew 10:35 is used to justify quarrels the flesh produced.
corruption_paragraphs: Read Galatians 5:19-21 and count: adultery, fornication, uncleanness and lasciviousness are four; hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife, seditions, heresies and envyings are eight. The sins that divide a church outnumber the sins of the body two to one in the apostle's own list, and they carry the same warning at the end of it. Yet a congregation will remove a man for immorality and tolerate for decades another whose temper and ambition have set brother against brother, on the grounds that he is merely difficult. Paul does not allow the distinction. Variance is a work of the flesh, and the flesh is what the believer has crucified with the affections and lusts.

Matthew 10:35 is the verse most often pressed into service by men whose quarrels are their own doing. Christ does divide households, and no one who has watched a family turn on a new convert doubts it. But He is describing the cost of confessing Him, not licensing a combative spirit, and the same Lord commands His people, as much as lieth in them, to live peaceably with all men. The test is straightforward and uncomfortable: is the division over Christ, or over me? Where a man is at variance with his family because he will not deny the Lord, he has Matthew 10 for comfort. Where he is at variance because he is proud and sharp-tongued, he has Galatians 5 for a warning.
roots_summary: Greek eris (G2054), strife or contention — Galatians 5:20, Romans 1:29, 1 Corinthians 1:11; dichazo (G1369), to set at variance — Matthew 10:35, its only occurrence.
roots_lines: Greek eris (G2054) — contention, debate; Galatians 5:20, Romans 1:29, 1 Corinthians 1:11, Philippians 1:15.
Greek dichazo (G1369) — to cut in two, to set at odds; Matthew 10:35, its only occurrence in the New Testament.
Greek zelos (G2205) — emulation, jealousy; Galatians 5:20, standing next to variance in the list.
Greek dichostasia (G1370) — sedition, division; Galatians 5:20, Romans 16:17 of them which cause divisions.
Galatians 5:24 gives the remedy: they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.
usage: “Hatred, variance, emulations, wrath, strife” — works of the flesh, and the majority of the list.
“I am come to set a man at variance against his father” — the cost of confessing Him.
The test is whether the division is over Christ, or over me.
